title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

reading.body:
This is an impersonation failure, in which an AI-generated video of a well-known financial figure was used to present an investment as that person's recommendation. The video is the lure, not the mechanism of loss. The fraud itself was carried out by people who took over the conversation afterwards.

The impersonation sat at the top of the funnel, in promotional content the victim saw before any transaction. From there the contact moved to WhatsApp, then to instructions to open several accounts, then to remote access to the victim's own computer, and finally to borrowing. The check that police pointed to was independent verification of who the victim was dealing with, along with confirming that the financial services provider was authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority. Nothing in that chain required the video to be convincing for long, only long enough to get the victim into a private channel.

What is not established is the identity of the celebrity, which police did not name, and any finding against the people behind the video, since the account comes from the Police Service of Northern Ireland and reporting rather than from a court.

reports.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

summary:
A person in the Ards and north Down area lost £250,000 in a scam that used an AI generated video of a well known financial figure. The Police Service of Northern Ireland said the video appeared to promote an investment with large returns. Police did not name the celebrity. BBC News NI reported seeing similar scams that used financial experts Martin Lewis, Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett. The victim invested a small amount, then was contacted on WhatsApp and urged to pay more.

The fraudsters persuaded the victim to open several accounts and gave them remote access to the victim's computer, saying they were helping with the investment. Police said the victim was encouraged to borrow money, and the funds went to accounts controlled by criminals. The PSNI called it a sophisticated and substantial fraud. Superintendent Joanne Gibson, chair of the Scamwise Partnership, urged people to stop and check financial activity and to talk with relatives about fraud. Police advised independently verifying who they are dealing with and checking that financial services providers are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority.
